q: Who wrote 'The State of the Prisons' in 1777 and is regarded as a pioneer of prison reform?
a: John Howard
Cesare Beccaria
Jeremy Bentham
Alexander Maconochie
r: John Howard, sheriff of Bedfordshire, exposed prison conditions and pushed for reform.
Beccaria wrote 'On Crimes and Punishments' on criminal law reform.
Bentham designed the Panopticon prison and developed utilitarianism.
Maconochie developed the mark system on Norfolk Island.
e: Howard's work led to reforms in sanitation, separation and supervision of prisoners.

q: Who introduced the mark system on Norfolk Island, a forerunner of parole?
a: Alexander Maconochie
Sir Walter Crofton
Zebulon Brockway
John Howard
r: Maconochie let prisoners earn marks for work and good conduct to shorten their stay.
Crofton developed the Irish system with tickets of leave.
Brockway ran the Elmira Reformatory with indeterminate sentences.
Howard was a prison reformer who wrote on prison conditions.
e: The mark system linked release to the prisoner's own effort.

q: By what name are the revised UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (2015) known?
a: Mandela Rules
Bangkok Rules
Tokyo Rules
Beijing Rules
r: The 2015 revision of the Standard Minimum Rules is named after Nelson Mandela.
The Bangkok Rules concern women prisoners and women offenders.
The Tokyo Rules concern non-custodial measures.
The Beijing Rules concern juvenile justice.
e: The Mandela Rules set minimum standards for prison management and treatment.

q: What do the UN Bangkok Rules (2010) cover?
a: The treatment of women prisoners and women offenders
The treatment of juveniles in conflict with the law
The use of non-custodial measures for all offenders
The extradition of prisoners between countries
r: The Bangkok Rules address the specific needs of women in prison and women offenders.
Juvenile justice is covered by the Beijing Rules.
Non-custodial measures are covered by the Tokyo Rules.
Extradition is covered by treaties, not by the Bangkok Rules.
e: The Bangkok Rules supplement the Mandela Rules.

q: How does retribution differ from deterrence as a justification for punishment?
a: Retribution punishes because it is deserved; deterrence aims to prevent future crime
Retribution aims to prevent crime; deterrence punishes because it is deserved
Retribution applies only to fines; deterrence only to imprisonment
Retribution and deterrence mean the same thing
r: Retribution looks back at the offense and imposes a deserved penalty; deterrence looks forward to discourage crime.
This reverses the two ideas.
Both justifications apply to many kinds of penalties.
They are distinct justifications.
e: Other justifications include incapacitation, rehabilitation and restoration.

q: What is the difference between general and specific deterrence?
a: General deters the public; specific deters the offender himself
General deters the offender; specific deters the public
General applies to men; specific applies to women
General applies to fines; specific to imprisonment
r: General deterrence warns society through the example of punishment; specific deterrence discourages the punished offender from repeating.
This reverses the two ideas.
Deterrence does not depend on sex.
Deterrence does not depend on the kind of penalty.
e: Certainty of punishment deters more than severity.

q: How does imprisoning a dangerous offender protect society through incapacitation?
a: It removes his ability to commit crimes in the community
It ensures that he will never think about crime again
It teaches the public about the law
It makes the victim forgive the offender
r: Incapacitation prevents crimes by physically removing the offender from society for a time.
Incapacitation does not change the offender's thoughts.
Teaching the public is general deterrence.
Forgiveness is part of restorative approaches, not incapacitation.
e: Incapacitation does not by itself reform the offender.

q: Why does the Indeterminate Sentence Law fix a minimum and a maximum term?
a: To individualize the penalty and allow parole once the minimum is served
To make every prisoner serve the maximum penalty
To let the prisoner choose the length of his sentence
To give judges power to change the sentence each year
r: Act 4103 aims to uplift and redeem offenders by allowing release on parole after the minimum, if they are fit.
The point is to allow release before the maximum when deserved.
Prisoners do not choose their sentences.
Judges do not revise sentences yearly.
e: The Board of Pardons and Parole decides on parole.

q: Why can Philippine courts not impose the death penalty today?
a: R.A. 9346 prohibited the imposition of the death penalty
The Constitution requires the death penalty for heinous crimes
The death penalty is imposed only by the Supreme Court
The death penalty applies only to foreigners
r: R.A. 9346 (2006) prohibited the death penalty and replaced it with reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment.
The Constitution does not require it; Congress may provide it only for heinous crimes.
No court may impose it while R.A. 9346 is in force.
No such distinction exists.
e: Those whose sentences were reduced to reclusion perpetua by R.A. 9346 are not eligible for parole.

q: What does Article III, Section 19(2) of the Constitution say about the treatment of prisoners?
a: Degrading punishment and subhuman facilities shall be dealt with by law
Prisoners lose all rights once they are convicted
Prisoners may be punished in any way the warden chooses
Prisoners must pay for the cost of their own detention
r: The provision directs that physical, psychological or degrading punishment and subhuman penal facilities be dealt with by law.
Prisoners keep their rights except those limited by their confinement.
Punishment inside prisons must follow the law and rules.
No constitutional rule requires prisoners to pay for detention.
e: Section 19(1) also bans excessive fines and cruel, degrading or inhuman punishment.

q: Why are accessory penalties not usually stated separately in the judgment?
a: The law deems them included with certain principal penalties
Accessory penalties are only imposed by the warden
Accessory penalties are always waived by the court
Accessory penalties apply only to light felonies
r: Article 73 presumes that accessory penalties are imposed whenever the court imposes the principal penalty to which they are attached.
Accessory penalties are imposed by law, not by the warden.
They are not waived; they follow by operation of law.
They attach to graver principal penalties, such as reclusion perpetua.
e: Examples include civil interdiction and perpetual absolute disqualification.

q: Why does modern penology give importance to rehabilitation?
a: Most prisoners return to society, so reform helps reduce repeat offending
Rehabilitation removes the need for any prison security
Rehabilitation means prisoners are never punished
Rehabilitation is cheaper than giving prisoners food
r: Since most prisoners will be released, preparing them to live lawfully protects the public.
Security remains necessary alongside rehabilitation.
Rehabilitation works within the sentence imposed.
Basic needs must still be provided; rehabilitation is not a substitute.
e: Programs include education, livelihood, counseling and values formation.

q: A person is sentenced by the RTC to ten years of imprisonment. Where should he serve his sentence?
a: In a BuCor national penitentiary
In a BJMP municipal jail
In a provincial jail
In a barangay detention cell
r: Under R.A. 10575, BuCor has custody of national (insular) prisoners sentenced to more than three years.
BJMP jails hold detainees and those with shorter sentences.
Provincial jails hold provincial prisoners with shorter sentences.
Barangays do not hold sentenced prisoners.
e: The commitment order directs the transfer of the convict to BuCor.
l: R.A. 10575 (Bureau of Corrections Act of 2013), Sec. 4

q: A person charged with theft in a city court is awaiting trial. Which agency holds him?
a: The BJMP, in the city jail
The BuCor, in a penal colony
The PNP, in a crime laboratory
The DSWD, in a youth center
r: The BJMP has jurisdiction over district, city and municipal jails, including detainees awaiting trial.
BuCor holds sentenced national prisoners.
The PNP does not hold detainees in crime laboratories.
The DSWD handles children, not adult detainees.
e: The BJMP is under the DILG.

q: Which office supervises and controls a provincial jail?
a: The provincial government
The BJMP regional office
The Bureau of Corrections
The National Police Commission
r: Provincial jails are under the provincial governments, headed by the governor.
The BJMP covers district, city and municipal jails.
BuCor runs national penitentiaries.
NAPOLCOM administers the PNP.
e: Provincial jails are part of the correction pillar at the provincial level.

q: At the change of shift, what should the outgoing and incoming jail guards do?
a: Do a joint headcount and turn over the keys and logbook
Leave the keys in the cell block for the next shift
Skip the headcount if the last shift was quiet
Let a trusted PDL hand over the keys
r: A joint count and formal turnover fix accountability for the PDLs, keys and equipment.
Keys must never be left where PDLs can reach them.
Headcounts are required every shift.
PDLs must never handle keys.
e: Discrepancies are reported at once.

q: A warden is told to let a trusted PDL hold the cell keys to save manpower. How should he decide?
a: Refuse; PDLs must never hold or handle keys
Agree, if the PDL has good behavior
Agree, but only during the day
Agree, if the PDL signs a receipt
r: Key control is a basic security rule; giving keys to PDLs invites escapes and abuses.
Good behavior does not make key control unnecessary.
The rule applies at all times.
A receipt does not cure the security risk.
e: Keys are kept in a controlled key box and issued only to authorized personnel.

q: A warden receives reliable information about a planned escape. What is the best decision?
a: Tighten security and conduct a surprise search (greyhound operation)
Ignore it until an escape attempt actually happens
Announce the information to all PDLs in a meeting
Release the PDLs involved to avoid trouble
r: Acting on the intelligence with stronger security and a surprise search can prevent the escape.
Waiting allows the plan to proceed.
Announcing it tips off the planners.
Release without a court order is illegal.
e: The warden also reports to higher headquarters.

q: A policy will apply to all national penitentiaries. Who issues it?
a: The BuCor Director General, under the DOJ
The Chief of the BJMP, under the DILG
The provincial governor
The Chief of the PNP
r: R.A. 10575 places BuCor under the DOJ, headed by a Director General.
The BJMP covers city, municipal and district jails.
Governors supervise provincial jails only.
The PNP has no authority over penitentiaries.
e: The Director General is assisted by Deputy Directors General.

q: A municipal jail is badly overcrowded. Which agency is responsible for addressing it?
a: The BJMP, under the DILG
The BuCor, under the DOJ
The PPA, under the DOJ
The DSWD
r: Municipal jails are under the BJMP, which is attached to the DILG.
BuCor runs national penitentiaries.
The PPA supervises probationers and parolees.
The DSWD handles children and social welfare.
e: Decongestion often needs coordination with the courts and prosecutors.

q: A jail's population is far above its capacity. Which plan best addresses it?
a: Coordinate with courts on pending cases and process PDLs' time allowances
Stop admitting PDLs, even with valid commitment orders
Release PDLs at random to reduce the number
Ignore the problem until a new jail is built
r: Decongestion uses legal means such as speedy trial coordination, paralegal help and timely processing of GCTA.
Jails must admit PDLs with valid commitment orders.
Release without legal basis is unlawful.
Overcrowding harms safety and health and must be acted on.
e: Paralegal programs help PDLs whose cases are delayed.

q: A jail officer is caught smuggling cellphones into the jail. What should the warden do?
a: Relieve him and file administrative and criminal cases
Warn him privately and let him continue
Transfer him without any investigation
Ignore it, since cellphones are not drugs
r: Accountability requires relief from duty pending investigation and the filing of proper charges.
A private warning does not address a serious violation.
Transfer without investigation passes on the problem.
Contraband of any kind threatens jail security.
e: Corruption of personnel is a major source of contraband.

q: A person is brought to the jail without a commitment order from the court. What should the jail do?
a: Refuse admission until a valid order is shown
Admit him now and ask for the order next month
Admit him if the arresting officer insists
Hold him in the jail lobby without records
r: A jail may hold a person only on a valid commitment order or other lawful authority.
Holding him without an order is illegal detention.
Insistence does not replace the legal requirement.
Unrecorded holding is unlawful and dangerous.
e: The commitment order states the legal basis for detention.

q: A newly committed PDL arrives at the jail. Which step comes before assigning him to a cell?
a: Search, booking and medical examination
Assignment to a livelihood program
Approval of his visitors' list
Release on recognizance
r: Admission includes a body search, booking (records, photographs, fingerprints) and a medical check before housing.
Programs come after admission and classification.
Visitors' lists come after admission.
Release requires a court order.
e: The PDL also undergoes orientation and classification.

q: A release order for a PDL arrives by fax late at night. What should the jail do before releasing him?
a: Verify the order's authenticity with the issuing court
Release him at once, since the fax looks official
Ignore the order until the PDL's family complains
Release him only if he pays a fee
r: Release orders must be verified to prevent escapes through fake documents.
A fax can be forged.
Valid orders must be acted on promptly once verified.
Release cannot depend on payment.
e: The jail also checks for other pending cases before release.

q: A visitor brings food for a PDL. What should the jail staff do?
a: Inspect the food and items before they are passed on
Pass it on without inspection, since it is only food
Refuse all food, since visitors may not bring any
Let the PDL inspect the food himself
r: Food and items are common ways to smuggle contraband, so they are inspected.
Food can hide contraband.
Rules usually allow food within limits.
PDLs cannot inspect their own items.
e: Visitors are also registered and searched under the jail's rules.

q: While escorting a high-risk PDL to court, the PDL asks to stop by his house. What should the escort do?
a: Refuse and go straight to the court
Allow a short stop if the PDL promises to behave
Allow it if the family pays for the fuel
Let the PDL decide the route
r: Escorts follow the authorized route without unauthorized stops, which could allow escape or ambush.
Promises do not change security rules.
Payment would be corruption.
The escort, not the PDL, controls movement.
e: High-risk PDLs are escorted with enough personnel and restraints.

q: The court orders a PDL's hearing to be held by videoconference. What should the jail do?
a: Arrange the remote appearance from a secure room in the jail
Bring the PDL to court anyway, ignoring the order
Postpone the hearing until the PDL is released
Let the PDL use his own cellphone for the hearing
r: Courts may allow remote appearances; the jail sets up the link from a secure place.
The court's order must be followed.
The jail has no power to postpone a hearing.
PDLs are not allowed personal cellphones.
e: Remote hearings reduce escort risks and costs.
l: Supreme Court guidelines on videoconferencing hearings

q: A PDL is found with a cellphone during a search. How should it be handled?
a: Confiscate and record it, and file a disciplinary case with a hearing
Let him keep it if he uses it only for family calls
Return it to him after a day
Punish him at once without any record
r: Contraband is seized and documented, and discipline follows due process.
Unauthorized phones are contraband regardless of their use.
Returning contraband defeats security.
Discipline without a record or hearing violates due process.
e: The source of the contraband is also investigated.

q: A PDL accused of fighting is placed in isolation without being told why or given a chance to explain. What is wrong with this?
a: Discipline requires notice and a hearing before a penalty
Nothing, since jail discipline needs no procedure
Isolation can only be ordered by a court
Fighting is not a disciplinary offense in jails
r: The Mandela Rules and jail regulations require that PDLs be told the charge and given a chance to be heard.
Discipline must follow due process.
Wardens may impose discipline through disciplinary boards.
Fighting is a disciplinary offense.
e: Prolonged solitary confinement is prohibited by the Mandela Rules.
l: UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (Mandela Rules), Rules 39-45

q: The evening headcount is one PDL short. What should the officers do first?
a: Lock down, recount, and report at once while searching
Wait until the morning count to see if he returns
Record the correct number to avoid trouble
Ask the other PDLs to find him
r: A discrepancy may mean an escape; lockdown, recount, immediate reporting and search are needed.
Delay gives an escapee more time.
Falsifying records is a serious offense.
PDLs cannot be given custodial tasks.
e: Escape plans are part of every jail's contingency planning.

q: Police bring a 16-year-old to a city jail for detention. What should the jail do?
a: Keep him away from adults; refer him to social welfare
Hold him in the same cell as adult detainees
Hold him in a separate cell for a few weeks
Admit him with adults if his parents agree
r: R.A. 9344 bars detaining children in jails with adults; they are turned over to social welfare or a Bahay Pag-asa.
Children must never be held with adults.
Jails are not proper facilities for children.
Parental agreement does not change the law.
e: Children in conflict with the law are handled under the juvenile justice system.

q: Why is containment the first priority when a riot breaks out in one cell block?
a: It keeps the riot from spreading and prevents escapes
It allows the rioters to calm down on their own
It lets the warden avoid reporting the incident
It ensures that all PDLs are released
r: Isolating the area protects the rest of the facility and the perimeter while the response is organized.
Containment is an active security measure.
Incidents must be reported.
Containment keeps PDLs secured, not released.
e: After containment, the crisis team plans how to restore order with minimum force.

q: Why should a jail notify the police and nearby units right after an escape?
a: Pursuit is most effective while the trail is fresh
The escapee will surely return on his own
Notification is needed only after a week
The police have no role in recapturing escapees
r: Early notice allows checkpoints and pursuit before the escapee gets far.
Escapees seldom return voluntarily.
Delay reduces the chance of recapture.
Police help in recapture operations.
e: Negligent guards may be liable under Article 224 of the Revised Penal Code.

q: Many PDLs fall ill after lunch. Why should samples of the food be kept?
a: To find the cause of the poisoning and fix responsibility
To serve the food again at the next meal
To show the food to visitors as an example
To throw it away later without testing
r: Testing the samples shows what caused the illness and who is accountable.
Suspect food must never be served again.
Display serves no purpose.
Discarding samples destroys evidence.
e: Sick PDLs receive medical care first.

q: Contraband keeps getting into a jail despite cell searches. Why should the warden study the entry points?
a: Contraband comes from outside, so its source must be closed
Cell searches are the only way to stop contraband
Contraband is made by the PDLs inside their cells
Entry points have no link to contraband
r: Repeated searches find contraband but do not stop it; controlling entry points stops the supply.
Searches alone treat the symptom.
Most contraband, such as phones, comes from outside.
Entry points are the main channel.
e: Staff corruption is often part of the problem.

q: PDLs take a guard hostage and demand to talk to the media. Which response is best?
a: Contain the area and let trained negotiators handle it
Give in to all of their demands at once to free the guard
Storm the area immediately without any plan
Open the gates so the PDLs can leave
r: Containment, negotiation and a coordinated crisis team give the best chance of a safe resolution.
Giving in to everything encourages future incidents.
An unplanned assault endangers the hostage.
Releasing PDLs is unlawful and dangerous.
e: Negotiation buys time to plan and to protect lives.

q: A fire breaks out in a jail at night. Which action is most appropriate?
a: Move the PDLs under guard to a set safe area, per the fire plan
Open all of the gates and let the PDLs run out on their own
Keep all cells locked until the fire is out
Wait for the morning shift before acting
r: A fire plan provides safe evacuation while keeping PDLs in custody.
Opening the gates leads to escapes and chaos.
Leaving PDLs locked in a fire endangers lives.
Delay can be deadly.
e: Fire drills prepare staff and PDLs for evacuation.

q: Which plan best prepares a jail for a strong earthquake?
a: Set safe areas inside the perimeter, hold drills, count after
Plan to release all of the PDLs whenever the ground shakes
Leave planning to the PDLs' leaders
Have no plan, since earthquakes cannot be predicted
r: Preparedness keeps PDLs safe and in custody during and after an earthquake.
Releasing PDLs is not a lawful response.
Planning is a duty of management.
Unpredictability is the reason to prepare.
e: PDLs who return after a calamity may earn a special time allowance for loyalty.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 98, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: A jail in a flood-prone area faces a strong typhoon. Which decision is best?
a: Transfer PDLs early to a safer facility, with stocks of food and water
Wait until the flood enters the cells before acting
Release the PDLs to their families during the typhoon
Move only the guards to safety
r: Early transfer, done lawfully, protects lives while keeping custody; supplies prepare for isolation.
Waiting risks drowning and escapes.
Release needs a lawful basis.
PDLs' lives must be protected too.
e: The courts are informed of transfers of detainees.

q: Which body recommends executive clemency and grants parole?
a: Board of Pardons and Parole
Parole and Probation Administration
Bureau of Corrections
National Police Commission
r: The Board of Pardons and Parole grants parole and recommends pardon and other clemency to the President.
The PPA supervises probationers and parolees.
BuCor runs national penitentiaries.
NAPOLCOM administers the PNP.
e: The Board is attached to the DOJ.

q: Which form of clemency postpones the execution of a sentence?
a: Reprieve
Commutation
Absolute pardon
Amnesty
r: A reprieve temporarily delays the execution of a sentence.
Commutation reduces the sentence.
Absolute pardon frees the convict from the penalty.
Amnesty wipes out the offense, usually political.
e: Reprieves were usually granted in death penalty cases.

q: What happens if a person granted a conditional pardon violates its conditions?
a: He may be rearrested to serve the rest of his sentence
Nothing, because a pardon cannot be withdrawn
His original conviction is erased
He is automatically placed on probation
r: The President may order rearrest and recommitment, and he may also be prosecuted under Article 159.
A conditional pardon depends on compliance with its conditions.
Violation revives, not erases, the penalty.
Probation is a separate court-granted privilege.
e: A conditional pardon is like a contract between the State and the grantee.

q: What does commutation of sentence do?
a: It reduces the penalty to a lighter one
It erases the crime as if it never happened
It postpones the sentence for a time
It sets the convict free under supervision
r: Commutation replaces the sentence with a lighter penalty or shorter term.
Erasing the offense is amnesty.
Postponing is a reprieve.
Release under supervision describes parole.
e: Commutation partially extinguishes criminal liability.

q: Why can the President not pardon an accused whose case is still on appeal?
a: The Constitution allows pardon only after final conviction
Pardon is allowed only for minor offenses
Only the Supreme Court may grant pardons
Pardon is allowed only before the case is filed
r: Article VII, Section 19 allows pardon only after conviction by final judgment.
Pardon may cover grave offenses too.
Pardon is an executive act, not a judicial one.
Pardon comes after, not before, conviction.
e: An accused who wants a pardon must first withdraw his appeal.

q: A law repeals the crime for which a PDL is serving his sentence. How does this affect him?
a: He benefits, as favorable penal laws apply retroactively
He must still serve the full sentence anyway
He benefits only if he pays a fine
He loses all his time allowances
r: Article 22 gives retroactive effect to penal laws favorable to the accused, unless he is a habitual criminal.
Favorable laws apply to those already serving.
No fine is required.
Repeal does not cancel earned allowances.
e: Decriminalization is one of the non-executive ways a sentence may end.

q: An accused is sentenced to four years of imprisonment and wants probation. When must he apply?
a: Within the period for perfecting an appeal
Any time while serving his sentence
Only after his appeal is decided
Within one year from conviction
r: The application must be filed with the trial court within the period for perfecting an appeal.
Probation is not available once he starts serving.
Generally, filing an appeal bars probation, except under R.A. 10707's rule on modified judgments.
No one-year period exists.
e: Filing an application for probation is a waiver of the right to appeal.
l: P.D. 968, Sec. 4, as amended by R.A. 10707

q: An accused is sentenced to eight years of imprisonment. Can he apply for probation?
a: No, the maximum term exceeds six years
Yes, if it is his first offense
Yes, if the victim agrees
No, unless he pays a bond
r: P.D. 968 disqualifies those sentenced to a maximum term of more than six years.
A first offense does not cure the disqualification.
The victim's consent does not make him eligible.
A bond does not make him eligible.
e: Other disqualifications include crimes against national security and prior convictions with certain penalties.
l: P.D. 968, Sec. 9, as amended by R.A. 10707

q: The trial court gave a non-probationable sentence, but on appeal it was reduced to a probationable one. Can the accused still apply?
a: Yes, based on the modified decision before it becomes final
No, because he has already appealed
No, because only the trial court's sentence counts
Yes, but only after serving half of the sentence
r: R.A. 10707 allows probation based on the modified, probationable judgment, applied for before it becomes final.
R.A. 10707 created this exception to the bar on appeal.
The modified decision is the one that counts.
No service is required first.
e: This corrected the harsh result when a wrongly heavy sentence was later reduced on appeal.
l: P.D. 968, Sec. 4, as amended by R.A. 10707

q: The court orders a post-sentence investigation. Within what period must the probation officer submit his report?
a: 60 days
15 days
30 days
90 days
r: The probation officer submits the report within 60 days from receipt of the order.
The court decides within 15 days after receiving the report.
Thirty days is not the period set by law.
Ninety days is longer than the law allows.
e: The investigation covers the offender's background, character and risk.

q: After probation is granted, within how many hours must the probationer present himself to the probation officer?
a: 72 hours
24 hours
48 hours
7 days
r: A mandatory condition is reporting within 72 hours of receiving the probation order.
Twenty-four hours is not the period in the law.
Forty-eight hours is not the period in the law.
Seven days is too long.
e: He must also report at least once a month thereafter.

q: A probationer was sentenced to one year of imprisonment. What is the longest probation period the court may set?
a: Two years
One year
Six years
Ten years
r: If the sentence is not more than one year, probation may not exceed two years.
The period may be up to two years, not limited to one.
Six years is the limit for longer sentences.
Ten years is beyond what the law allows.
e: For sentences above one year, probation may not exceed six years.

q: A probationer repeatedly fails to report and is seen with known drug dealers. What may happen?
a: The court may issue a warrant and, after a hearing, revoke probation
The probation officer may jail him without any court order
Nothing, since probation cannot be revoked
He is given a new probation automatically
r: On violation, the court may order arrest, hold a summary hearing, and revoke or modify probation.
Only the court may order arrest and revocation.
Probation may be revoked for violations.
No automatic new probation exists.
e: An order revoking probation is not appealable.

q: A person is convicted of selling dangerous drugs under Section 5 of R.A. 9165. Can he apply for probation?
a: No, drug traffickers are disqualified from probation
Yes, if the drugs were small in amount
Yes, if he is a first-time offender
No, unless the PDEA agrees
r: Section 24 of R.A. 9165 disqualifies those convicted of drug trafficking or pushing from probation.
The amount does not lift the disqualification for sale.
First offense does not lift the disqualification.
PDEA's agreement has no effect on eligibility.
e: First-time minor offenders for drug use may get suspended sentence or probation under R.A. 9165.

q: A probationer has completed his probation and the court orders his final discharge. What is the effect?
a: His civil rights return and his liability for it ends
He must still serve the original prison sentence in full
He remains under supervision for life
He can no longer be employed by government
r: Final discharge restores civil rights lost by the conviction and totally extinguishes criminal liability for that offense.
Probation replaces service of the sentence.
Supervision ends with final discharge.
His rights are restored, not further limited.
e: Civil liability to the victim is a separate matter.

q: A respected resident of a remote town is appointed to help a probation officer supervise probationers there. What is his role?
a: Volunteer probation aide
Parole officer (PPA)
Probation officer (PPA)
Jail officer
r: Volunteer probation aides assist probation officers in supervising probationers in the community.
Parole officers supervise parolees and are employees of the PPA.
Probation officers are employees of the PPA.
Jail officers work inside jails.
e: Volunteers extend the reach of the probation system.

q: A PDL is serving an indeterminate sentence of 6 years and 1 day to 12 years. When may he first be considered for parole?
a: After serving the minimum of 6 years and 1 day
After serving the maximum of 12 years
After serving one year
Only after a presidential pardon
r: Under Act 4103, the Board may grant parole once the PDL has served the minimum and is found fit for release.
Serving the maximum means full service, not parole.
One year is below the minimum.
Parole is granted by the Board, not through pardon.
e: Good conduct time allowances count toward the period served.

q: A PDL is serving reclusion perpetua for murder. Is he eligible for parole under the Indeterminate Sentence Law?
a: No, reclusion perpetua is not covered by the law
Yes, after he has served at least ten years
Yes, as long as he keeps good behavior
No, unless he is over sixty years old
r: The ISL does not apply to those sentenced to life imprisonment or reclusion perpetua; R.A. 9346 also bars their parole.
No such ten-year rule applies under the ISL.
Good behavior does not make the ISL apply.
Age does not make the ISL apply.
e: Such PDLs may seek executive clemency instead.

q: A habitual delinquent is sentenced to imprisonment. How does the Indeterminate Sentence Law apply to him?
a: It does not apply; habitual delinquents are excluded
It applies with an extra reward of parole
It applies only if he pleads guilty
It applies once he reaches old age
r: Act 4103 excludes habitual delinquents from its benefits.
Habitual delinquents get no special parole reward.
A guilty plea does not remove the exclusion.
Age does not remove the exclusion.
e: Other exclusions include those who escaped or violated a conditional pardon.

q: A convict is sentenced to ten months of imprisonment. Does the Indeterminate Sentence Law apply?
a: No, it does not apply to terms not exceeding one year
Yes, he gets a minimum and maximum term
Yes, he may be paroled after one month
No, because he must apply for probation instead
r: The ISL excludes those whose maximum term does not exceed one year; a straight penalty is imposed.
Short terms are not split into minimum and maximum.
Parole under the ISL is not available for such terms.
He may apply for probation, but that is a separate matter from the ISL.
e: Probation may be available for him if he qualifies.

q: A PDL's records show he has served his minimum term with good conduct. Which body decides whether he will be paroled?
a: Board of Pardons and Parole
Parole and Probation Administration
Trial court that convicted him
Bureau of Corrections
r: The BPP evaluates and grants parole.
The PPA supervises parolees after release.
The trial court does not grant parole.
BuCor submits records but does not grant parole.
e: The institution forwards the PDL's carpeta and prison record to the Board.

q: After his release on parole, who supervises the parolee?
a: A parole and probation officer of the PPA
The warden of his former jail
The barangay captain of his area
The judge who convicted him
r: The Parole and Probation Administration supervises parolees through its officers.
The warden's custody ends at release.
Barangay officials may help but are not the supervisors.
Judges do not supervise parolees.
e: The parolee reports regularly to his supervising officer.

q: A parolee commits a new offense while on parole. What may the Board of Pardons and Parole do?
a: Order his arrest and recommitment for the rest of his term
Nothing, since a grant of parole can never be revoked
Give him a second parole at once as a final chance
Reduce his sentence as a warning
r: Act 4103 lets the Board order the rearrest of a parolee who violates his conditions, to serve the remaining sentence.
Parole can be revoked for violations.
There is no automatic second parole.
Violation leads to recommitment, not reduction.
e: He may also be prosecuted for the new offense.

q: A parolee still has four years left on his maximum sentence. How long does his parole supervision last?
a: Until his maximum term ends, unless finally released earlier
For six months only from the date of his release
For the rest of his life, even after the maximum term
Until he finds a job and can support himself
r: Supervision covers the unexpired portion of the maximum sentence; the Board may issue a final release earlier for good conduct.
Six months is not the period under the law.
Supervision ends when the maximum term expires.
Employment does not end supervision.
e: A final certificate of release ends his supervision.

q: Which records of the PDL does the institution send to the Board of Pardons and Parole for its review?
a: The carpeta and prison record
The PDL's social media posts
The PDL's bank statements
The PDL's school report cards
r: The carpeta (case file) and prison record show the sentence, conduct and program participation.
Social media posts are not the institutional record.
Bank statements are not part of the review.
School records are not the institutional record.
e: Incomplete records often delay parole review.

q: A parolee wants to move to another province for work. What should he do?
a: Get prior approval so his supervision can be transferred
Move at once without telling anyone
Stop reporting, since he will be far away
Ask his former jail warden for permission
r: Parolees must obtain approval to change residence, and supervision is transferred to the new area.
Moving without approval violates his conditions.
Failing to report is a violation.
The warden no longer has authority over him.
e: The conditions of parole are stated in the release document.

q: Under R.A. 10592, how many days of good conduct time allowance per month are earned in the first two years?
a: 20 days
23 days
25 days
30 days
r: Twenty days per month are granted during the first two years.
Twenty-three days apply from the third to the fifth year.
Twenty-five days apply from the sixth to the tenth year.
Thirty days apply from the eleventh year onward.
e: GCTA applies to both preventive imprisonment and service of sentence.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 97, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: Who may grant good conduct time allowances under R.A. 10592?
a: The BuCor Director, BJMP Chief or jail warden
The trial judge who convicted the PDL
The President of the Philippines only
The barangay captain where the PDL lives
r: Article 99, as amended, vests this authority in the Director of BuCor, the Chief of the BJMP and wardens of provincial, district, city or municipal jails.
Judges do not grant GCTA.
The President grants clemency, not GCTA.
Barangay officials have no role in GCTA.
e: Grants are made through management screening committees.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 99, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: Why can a time allowance not be taken back once it has been granted?
a: The law says allowances once granted shall not be revoked
Allowances are always granted by the President alone
Allowances are only temporary favors
Allowances are given only after release
r: Article 99, as amended, provides that time allowances once granted shall not be revoked.
Allowances are granted by correctional authorities.
Once granted, they are permanent.
Allowances are credited during detention and service.
e: Misbehavior affects future grants, not those already given.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 99, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: What extra allowance may a PDL earn by teaching, studying or mentoring?
a: 15 days per month, on top of GCTA
5 days per year, instead of GCTA
30 days per year, only at release
None, because only work counts
r: R.A. 10592 adds 15 days per month for teaching, studying or mentoring service.
The allowance is monthly and additional to GCTA.
It is credited monthly, not only at release.
Teaching, studying and mentoring are expressly rewarded.
e: This encourages participation in education and mentoring programs.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 97, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: Which of the following partially extinguishes criminal liability?
a: Good conduct allowances
Absolute pardon
Death of the convict
Amnesty
r: Article 94 lists conditional pardon, commutation and good conduct allowances as partial extinction.
Absolute pardon totally extinguishes liability.
Death totally extinguishes criminal liability.
Amnesty totally extinguishes liability.
e: Total extinction is covered by Article 89.

q: Why is an absolute pardon a total, but a conditional pardon only a partial, extinction of criminal liability?
a: A conditional pardon can be undone if its conditions are broken
A conditional pardon is granted only by the trial courts
An absolute pardon applies only to light offenses
An absolute pardon is granted only after death
r: The conditional pardon's effect depends on compliance, so liability is only partly extinguished.
Both pardons are executive acts.
Absolute pardons may cover grave offenses.
Pardons are granted to living convicts.
e: Violation of a conditional pardon is punished under Article 159.

q: A detainee who agreed in writing to follow the rules has been held for two years. The maximum penalty for his offense is two years. What should happen?
a: He should be released, though his trial continues
He must stay until the trial ends
He must serve two more years after conviction
He should be transferred to BuCor
r: Article 29 orders release when preventive imprisonment equals the possible maximum penalty, without prejudice to the trial.
Continued detention would exceed the possible penalty.
He has already been credited the full period.
There is no basis to transfer him.
e: This prevents detainees from being held longer than any sentence they could receive.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 29, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: A detainee did not agree to follow the rules for convicted prisoners and spent 20 months in preventive imprisonment. How much is credited to his sentence?
a: 16 months
20 months
10 months
None
r: Without the written agreement, he is credited with four-fifths of the period: 4/5 x 20 = 16 months.
Full credit requires the written agreement.
One-half is not the rule.
He still gets partial credit.
e: The agreement is made in writing with the assistance of counsel.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 29, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: During an earthquake, a PDL left the jail and returned within 48 hours after the calamity was declared over. What allowance may he receive?
a: A deduction of one-fifth of his sentence
A deduction of two-fifths of his sentence
No deduction, since he left the jail
Immediate release
r: Article 98 grants one-fifth for PDLs who evaded during a calamity and gave themselves up within 48 hours after it passed.
Two-fifths is for those who chose to stay.
The law rewards his return.
The allowance reduces the sentence; it does not mean release.
e: This is the special time allowance for loyalty.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 98, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: During a calamity, a PDL chose to stay in the jail even though he could have left. What allowance may he receive?
a: A deduction of two-fifths of his sentence
A deduction of one-fifth of his sentence
No deduction, since he did nothing
An additional 15 days per month
r: R.A. 10592 grants two-fifths to PDLs who chose to stay despite the calamity.
One-fifth is for those who left and returned.
Choosing to stay is rewarded by law.
Fifteen days per month is the allowance for teaching, studying or mentoring.
e: The reward recognizes loyalty during emergencies.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 98, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: A recidivist detainee asks for credit for his preventive imprisonment. How should his request be evaluated?
a: Deny it; recidivists are excluded from the credit
Grant full credit, since all detainees are covered
Grant double credit, since he has more experience
Grant it only if his first case was minor
r: Article 29, as amended, excludes recidivists, habitual delinquents, escapees and persons charged with heinous crimes.
Not all detainees are covered.
There is no double credit in the law.
The exclusion does not depend on the first offense.
e: Exclusions are applied as the law states them.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 29, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: A warden grants 20 days per month of GCTA to a PDL in his fourth year of good conduct. Is this correct?
a: No; from the third to the fifth year it is 23 days
Yes; it is 20 days for every year
No; it should be 30 days in the fourth year
Yes; the warden may choose any number
r: Article 97 grants 23 days per month from the third to the fifth year.
Twenty days apply only to the first two years.
Thirty days apply from the eleventh year.
The allowance is fixed by law.
e: Correct computation affects the PDL's release date.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 97, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: A jail officer says that a PDL's earned time allowances will be cancelled because he misbehaved this month. How should this be evaluated?
a: Incorrect; granted allowances cannot be revoked
Correct; allowances can be revoked at any time
Correct; misbehavior cancels all past allowances
Incorrect; misbehavior has no effect at all
r: Article 99 makes granted allowances irrevocable, though misbehavior can bar future grants.
Granted allowances cannot be revoked.
Past grants stay; only future grants are affected.
Misbehavior can still affect future allowances and discipline.
e: Disciplinary measures for the misbehavior follow due process.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 99, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: A PDL in his eleventh year of good conduct also teaches in the jail school. How many days per month may he earn in total?
a: 45 days
30 days
25 days
15 days
r: From the eleventh year he earns 30 days of GCTA, plus 15 days for teaching: 45 days per month.
Thirty days is GCTA alone.
Twenty-five days apply to the sixth to tenth years.
Fifteen days is the teaching allowance alone.
e: Both allowances are credited together.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 97, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: Which treatment approach uses the community of PDLs itself as the main agent of change?
a: Therapeutic Community
Solitary confinement
Electroconvulsive therapy
Work release only
r: The Therapeutic Community is a self-help, social learning approach where the community helps each member change.
Solitary confinement isolates, which is the opposite.
Electroconvulsive therapy is a psychiatric treatment, not a correctional modality.
Work release is a program, not a community-based treatment model.
e: The BJMP and BuCor use the Therapeutic Community Modality Program.

q: Which component of the Therapeutic Community teaches job skills for life after release?
a: Vocational and survival skills
Behavior management
Emotional and psychological
Intellectual and spiritual
r: The vocational and survival skills component prepares PDLs for work and daily living.
Behavior management shapes conduct through rules and consequences.
The emotional and psychological component deals with feelings.
The intellectual and spiritual component develops thinking and values.
e: The four components work together in the TC program.

q: Why does behavior management in the Therapeutic Community use rewards and sanctions?
a: To reinforce good behavior and discourage harmful behavior
To punish PDLs as harshly as possible
To let PDLs do as they please without rules
To decide which PDLs will be released
r: Behavior shaping applies operant conditioning: rewards strengthen prosocial behavior and sanctions weaken harmful behavior.
The aim is change, not harshness.
Clear rules are central to behavior management.
Release is decided by courts and the Board.
e: Consistent consequences make the rules meaningful.

q: What does the emotional and psychological component of the Therapeutic Community address?
a: Helping PDLs understand and manage feelings
Training PDLs in carpentry and welding skills
Teaching PDLs to read and write
Organizing sports competitions
r: This component helps PDLs handle emotions through counseling and group sessions.
Vocational skills belong to another component.
Literacy belongs to the intellectual component.
Sports belong to recreational programs.
e: Unmanaged emotions often contribute to offending.

q: Why are education and spiritual programs part of rehabilitation?
a: They change thinking and values and improve chances of a lawful life
They replace the need for any security in the jail
They are only ways to pass the time
They are required for every PDL's release by law
r: Education and values formation help PDLs think differently and find lawful work.
Security is still needed.
These programs have rehabilitative aims.
They help, but release follows legal processes.
e: The Alternative Learning System is offered in many jails.

q: Why does cognitive therapy focus on a PDL's 'thinking errors'?
a: Changing distorted thinking helps change behavior
Thinking has no link to behavior
It aims to make PDLs forget their crimes
It is used only for PDLs with physical illnesses
r: Cognitive approaches hold that how people think shapes how they act, so correcting distortions changes behavior.
Thought and behavior are closely linked.
The aim is change, not forgetting.
It is used for behavior, not physical illness.
e: Examples of thinking errors include blaming others and minimizing harm.

q: A PDL never finished high school. Which program should the jail offer him?
a: Alternative Learning System (ALS) classes
Solitary confinement for reflection
Early release to study outside
Work in the jail kitchen only
r: ALS lets PDLs complete basic education inside the facility.
Isolation does not provide education.
Release needs a legal basis.
Kitchen work alone does not give education.
e: Studying may also earn time allowances.
l: Revised Penal Code, Art. 97, as amended by R.A. 10592

q: A PDL has a long history of drug dependence. Which program suits him?
a: Therapeutic Community modality or drug rehabilitation program
A longer stay in isolation
No program, since drugs are not allowed in jail
Transfer to a jail with no programs
r: The TC modality and drug rehabilitation programs address addiction and behavior.
Isolation does not treat dependence.
Absence of drugs does not end dependence.
Moving him to a place without programs ignores his needs.
e: Untreated dependence raises the risk of relapse and reoffending.

q: A PDL will be released in six months. Which program should start now?
a: Pre-release preparation, with job and family reintegration
Nothing, since release will take care of itself
Transfer to a maximum security facility
Suspension of all his visits
r: Pre-release programs prepare PDLs for work, housing and family life after release.
Unprepared release increases the risk of reoffending.
Higher security is not needed for reintegration.
Family contact supports reintegration.
e: Coordination with the PPA, LGUs and families is part of reintegration.

q: PDLs make handicrafts that are sold at the jail's outlet. What is the purpose of this program?
a: To build skills and earn income through livelihood
To make the jail a profitable business for staff
To punish PDLs with forced labor
To keep PDLs away from their families
r: Livelihood programs build skills and let PDLs earn for themselves and their families.
Earnings are not for the personal profit of staff.
Participation is part of rehabilitation, not punishment.
Livelihood helps support families.
e: Earnings are handled under the facility's rules.

q: A PDL complains that he has been denied medical care for weeks. What should the jail do?
a: Give him access to proper medical care at once
Tell him that PDLs have no right to medical care
Make him pay before seeing a doctor
Wait until his release to treat him
r: The Mandela Rules require health care for PDLs equal to that in the community.
PDLs keep their right to health care.
Basic health care must not depend on payment.
Delay can worsen his condition.
e: Health care is a State responsibility for persons in custody.
l: UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (Mandela Rules), Rule 24

q: A PDL of a minority faith wants to practice his religion. How should the jail respond?
a: Allow and assist it within security rules
Forbid it, since only one religion is allowed
Allow it only if he converts first
Ignore the request completely
r: The Mandela Rules protect religious practice, subject to security needs.
Freedom of religion covers all faiths.
Forced conversion violates religious freedom.
Ignoring the request denies his rights.
e: Religious programs also support rehabilitation.
l: UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (Mandela Rules), Rules 65-66

q: A PDL's family lives far away and cannot visit often. How can the jail help maintain contact?
a: Arrange regulated contact, such as video calls
Ban all contact with them until he is released
Allow him to keep a personal cellphone
Tell him to forget his family
r: Regulated contact, including video visits, keeps family ties while keeping security.
Family ties support rehabilitation.
Personal cellphones are contraband.
Family support reduces reoffending.
e: Video visitation was widely used in jails during the pandemic.

q: Under the Mandela Rules, how much outdoor exercise should PDLs who are not doing outdoor work have each day?
a: At least one hour, if weather permits
At least ten minutes per week
None, since exercise is a privilege
Only on national holidays
r: Rule 23 provides at least one hour of suitable exercise in the open air daily, if weather permits.
Ten minutes a week is far below the standard.
Exercise is a minimum standard, not a privilege.
It is daily, not only on holidays.
e: Exercise supports physical and mental health.
l: UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (Mandela Rules), Rule 23

q: A woman PDL gives birth while in custody. How should decisions about her infant be made?
a: Based on the best interests of the child
Based only on the jail's convenience
The infant must always be removed at once
The infant must stay with her until age ten
r: The Bangkok Rules require decisions on children staying with mothers to be based on the child's best interests.
Convenience is not the standard.
Automatic removal ignores the child's interests.
No fixed age applies; the child's interests decide.
e: Facilities must meet the needs of mothers and infants.

q: A PDL with a known mental illness acts strangely and refuses meals. How should the jail respond?
a: Refer him to mental health services for assessment
Punish him for disobedience
Ignore him until he behaves normally
Transfer him to a crowded cell
r: Symptoms of illness need assessment and treatment, not punishment.
Punishing illness worsens it and violates rights.
Ignoring him risks his health.
Crowding may make his condition worse.
e: R.A. 11036 protects the rights of persons with mental health conditions.

q: Why does the Therapeutic Community use a 'family' structure with peer responsibility?
a: Peers confront and support each other in the community
It saves the jail from hiring any staff
It lets the strongest PDLs control all the others
It is only a way to group PDLs by age
r: The TC uses the community as method: members hold each other accountable and model change.
Staff still guide and supervise the program.
The TC is structured to prevent abuse by strong members.
Grouping is by program structure, not just age.
e: Social learning inside the community supports lasting change.

q: Why do reintegration programs involve the PDL's family and community before release?
a: Support and acceptance after release reduce reoffending
Families must pay for the PDL's programs
Communities decide whether the PDL will be released
Families are needed only to sign papers
r: Family and community support help with housing, work and acceptance, which lower recidivism.
Programs are not paid for by families.
Release is decided by courts and the Board.
Their role goes beyond paperwork.
e: Stigma can push former PDLs back into crime.

q: Which program design is most likely to reduce reoffending after release?
a: Continuing aftercare with job placement and supervision
Release with no follow-up or support
Longer sentences for every PDL
Banning former PDLs from their barangays
r: Aftercare and job support address the needs that often lead to reoffending.
Unsupported release leaves needs unmet.
Longer sentences alone do not reduce recidivism.
Banishment increases marginalization.
e: The PPA and LGUs share responsibility for aftercare.

q: A town proposes to bar all former PDLs from any job in the local government. How should this policy be evaluated?
a: It hinders reintegration; a case-by-case review is fairer
It is ideal, since former PDLs cannot change
It is required by the Constitution
It has no effect on reintegration
r: Blanket bans increase stigma and unemployment, which raise reoffending; case-by-case review balances safety and fairness.
Rehabilitation assumes people can change.
The Constitution does not require such bans.
Employment strongly affects reintegration.
e: Some positions may lawfully have specific requirements, but blanket exclusion is broad.
